meta.title: Who really said "To live is to suffer, to survive is to find meaning in the suffering"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Frankl and not Nietzsche: the line is from Gordon W. Allport's preface to Man's Search for Meaning, first published by Beacon Press in 1959.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'To live is to suffer, to survive is to find meaning in the suffering'?
meta.ogDescription: The sentence sits inside Frankl's book — but in Gordon W. Allport's 1959 preface, not in Frankl's own text. Verified against the Beacon Press edition.

answer.label: Not Viktor Frankl — actually Gordon W. Allport
answer.sourceLine: The sentence is Allport’s, not Frankl’s. It appears verbatim in the preface Allport wrote for the first English edition of Frankl’s memoir, published as From Death-Camp to Existentialism (Beacon Press, 1959) and reissued as Man’s Search for Meaning: “It is here that we encounter the central theme of existentialism: to live is to suffer, to survive is to find meaning in the suffering.” Allport was summarising Frankl’s argument in his own words — which is why the line rides inside Frankl’s book while never being written by him.

source.heading: The preface, not the memoir

source.excerpt: But these moments of comfort do not establish the will to live unless they help the prisoner make larger sense out of his apparently senseless suffering. It is here that we encounter the central theme of existentialism: to live is to suffer, to survive is to find meaning in the suffering.
trail: Quote Investigator has no article on this line, so the check runs against the book itself. Catalogue records for the first American edition list the volume as Beacon Press, Boston, 1959, translated by Ilse Lasch, preface by Gordon W. Allport ↗.
The sentence appears verbatim in that preface. A dedicated misquotation write-up reproduces the full paragraph from the Beacon Press printing ↗, matching the text read for this page word for word.
Frankl’s own nearest formulation is a different sentence in the body of the book: “If there is a meaning in life at all, then there must be a meaning in suffering” ↗.
Wikipedia’s account of the book confirms the 1946 German original, the 1959 English title, and that Allport wrote a preface to it ↗.
source.excerptNote: Allport’s paragraph continues with “If there is a purpose in life at all, there must be a purpose in suffering and in dying,” and closes by noting that Frankl is fond of quoting Nietzsche — the adjacency that almost certainly seeded the Nietzsche credit.

author.name: Gordon W. Allport
author.heading: Who actually wrote it
author.bio: Gordon Willard Allport was an American psychologist and a founding figure of personality psychology, on the Harvard faculty from 1930 until his death in 1967 and a former editor of the Journal of Abnormal and Social Psychology. He is best known for trait theory and for The Nature of Prejudice. His preface to Viktor Frankl’s concentration-camp memoir did more than any other single piece of writing to introduce logotherapy to American readers — and, unintentionally, produced one of the most-quoted sentences in the self-help canon.

misattribution.heading: Two wrong names, one real one
misattribution.intro: This line is credited to two different men who did not write it, and almost never to the man who did.

items.why: Usually in the variant “to survive is to find some meaning in the suffering,” which circulates on quotation sites under Nietzsche’s name — one Goodreads entry alone carries 923 likes ↗. No work of Nietzsche’s contains it; the credit appears to be an artefact of Allport ending the same paragraph by quoting Nietzsche.

The sentence really is inside Frankl’s book, which makes the credit feel safe — and quotation databases repeat it, filing the line under Frankl with the 1959 edition as its source ↗. But it belongs to the preface, and Frankl did not write the preface.

Frankl’s own formulation of the idea is longer and differently phrased: “If there is a meaning in life at all, then there must be a meaning in suffering” ↗. The thought is his; the famous compression is not.

misattribution.truthLine: The wording is Gordon W. Allport’s, from the preface he wrote for the 1959 Beacon Press first English edition ↗ of Frankl’s memoir.

context.heading: How a preface became a proverb
lead: Frankl’s memoir was written in German in 1946 as Ein Psychologe erlebt das Konzentrationslager. When Beacon Press brought it to American readers in 1959 as From Death-Camp to Existentialism, it arrived with a preface by Gordon W. Allport — then one of the most influential psychologists in the United States — whose endorsement was the book’s passport into American psychology. Allport used that preface to compress Frankl’s argument into a single memorable clause, and readers have been quoting the compression ever since.

Frankl did make the underlying claim, in his own words and at greater length: “If there is a meaning in life at all, then there must be a meaning in suffering.” What he never wrote is the tighter, more aphoristic sentence that now circulates under his name — or, more often still, under Nietzsche’s. It is a clean example of how front matter escapes a book: a summariser’s phrasing outruns the author’s own.
detailsBody: Allport’s paragraph ends by noting that Frankl is fond of quoting Nietzsche — “He who has a why to live can bear with almost any how.” A reader skimming the page finds an existentialist-sounding aphorism a few lines above a Nietzsche citation, and the two fuse. The variant that dominates search results, “to survive is to find some meaning in the suffering,” is the Nietzsche-credited form.

Nietzsche did write near this territory — on suffering being willed when a meaning for it is shown — but that is a different sentence in a different book, and no Nietzsche text contains the wording in circulation.
context.pull: Allport was paraphrasing Frankl. The paraphrase is what survived.

sourcesVerified.claim: The exact sentence 'to live is to suffer, to survive is to find meaning in the suffering' appears in Gordon W. Allport's preface to Man's Search for Meaning, and the preface is signed GORDON W. ALLPORT; the volume's copyright line reads (c) 1959, 1962, 1984, 1992 by Viktor E. Frankl, Beacon Press.

The line is misattributed to Nietzsche and to Frankl; it appears only in the preface of Man's Search for Meaning, which was written by Gordon Allport, a Harvard psychology professor and former editor of the Journal of Abnormal and Social Psychology; the page reproduces the full preface paragraph.

The first American edition, From Death-Camp to Existentialism: A Psychiatrist's Path to a New Therapy, was published by Beacon Press, Boston, 1959, translated by Ilse Lasch, with a preface by Gordon W. Allport.
Internet Archive holds a lending copy of 'From death-camp to existentialism; a psychiatrist's path to a new therapy' by Viktor E. Frankl (1905-1997), Beacon Press, Boston, 1959.

The German original was published in 1946 as Ein Psychologe erlebt das Konzentrationslager; the first English translation was titled From Death-Camp to Existentialism; Gordon Allport wrote a preface to the book.
Gordon Allport lived 11 November 1897 to 9 October 1967, was American, served on the Harvard faculty from 1930 to 1967, and is a founding figure of personality psychology.
The variant 'To live is to suffer, to survive is to find some meaning in the suffering' is published under Friedrich Nietzsche's name and carries 923 likes.

LibQuotes files the sentence 'It is here that we encounter the central theme of existentialism: to live is to suffer, to survive is to find meaning in the suffering' under Viktor Frankl, citing From Death-camp to Existentialism (1959 edition).
LibQuotes also files 'To live is to suffer, to survive is to find meaning in the suffering' under Gordon Allport, Man's Search For Meaning, with his dates 11 November 1897 - 9 October 1967.
Goodreads attributes 'If there is a meaning in life at all, then there must be a meaning in suffering' to Viktor E. Frankl, Man's Search for Meaning.
Viktor Emil Frankl was an Austrian neurologist, psychiatrist, philosopher and Holocaust survivor, 26 March 1905 to 2 September 1997, who founded logotherapy.
